quote: So here’s a reply to that philosopher’s scenario, which I have yet to hear any philosopher’s victim give:
content: This reply is R. M. Hare's two-level utilitarianism, published in Moral Thinking (1981; book, no DOI) and widely discussed since. Hare distinguished "archangels," who can calculate consequences perfectly and should act on them, from "proles," humans who should follow well-chosen intuitive rules because their case-by-case calculations are unreliable and self-serving. He explicitly used this to explain why people are right to resist trolley-style conclusions. The essay's "society of Artificial Intelligences" is Hare's archangel. The reply has been given, and the objections to it are well known.

quote: The tendency to be corrupted by power is a specific biological adaptation, supported by specific cognitive circuits, built into us by our genes for a clear evolutionary reason.
content: The essay opened with "Humans may have evolved" such a structure. A few paragraphs later the hypothesis has become a "specific biological adaptation" with "specific cognitive circuits." No study, circuit or evolutionary history is cited. The psychology of power is a real literature, but it rests largely on laboratory priming and correlational designs whose claims to establish cause and effect have been sharply criticized (Sturm & Antonakis 2015), and it identifies no dedicated circuit. A speculative just-so story has been promoted to fact to support the claim that an AI couldn't fail the same way.

quote: I wouldn’t endorse it as a principle for a society of AIs that make well-calibrated estimates.
content: The next essay contradicts this. "Ethical Injunctions" argues that an AI whose goals may be subtly wrong should shut itself down rather than act on a conclusion like "deceive my programmers," because it is more likely to be malfunctioning than right. In other words, AIs have their own corrupted hardware, in the form of mis-specified objectives. Specification gaming and reward hacking, now documented in many systems, are exactly that. The claim that AIs, lacking biology, wouldn't need deontological constraints doesn't survive the book's own analysis of how AIs fail.

quote: “The end does not justify the means” is just consequentialist reasoning at one meta-level up.
content: This is indirect or rule consequentialism, and it faces a well-known dilemma. If the rule is justified only by its consequences, then whenever you are confident that breaking it has better consequences, the theory tells you to break it. That is the "rule worship" objection Smart (1956) pressed against restricted utilitarianism. If you must follow the rule even then, it is no longer justified by consequences. The next essay raises exactly this question ("can't we just redo the calculation?") and answers with a warning about cleverness rather than an argument.

quote: then I don’t call it an alarm light, if an AI says that the right thing to do is sacrifice one to save five
content: An AI that concludes it should kill an innocent person to save five, and acts on it, is close to the paradigm of what AI safety work tries to prevent: an autonomous system overriding a constraint on the strength of its own consequentialist calculation. Research on corrigibility aims at systems that defer to human oversight precisely when their own calculations recommend drastic action (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017). "I don't call it an alarm light" is the attitude the author's later work warned against.
